title: Infantile haemangioma (strawberry mark)
summary: A benign vascular tumour that appears in the first weeks, grows fast for a few months, then slowly involutes. Refer high-risk sites early (ideally by about 4 weeks), while propranolol works best.

what: An **infantile haemangioma (IH)** is a benign vascular **tumour** of infancy. It is absent or a faint mark at birth, **grows rapidly** (mostly in the first 1–3 months, largely complete by about 5 months), plateaus, then **involutes** over years. About **4–10%** of infants are affected.

list: Clonal endothelial proliferation, **GLUT-1 positive** (unlike malformations and congenital haemangiomas).
Risk factors: prematurity, low birth weight, female sex, multiple pregnancy, placental anomalies.

head: Type
Appearance
rows: Bluish, rubbery swelling under the skin

features: Haemangiomas can occur anywhere, most often on the head and neck. **5 or more** skin haemangiomas raise concern for **liver haemangiomas**. White surface change can herald **ulceration**.

figure.caption: Natural history of infantile haemangioma: appearance (0–2 weeks), rapid growth (1–6 months), slow involution, and completion (5–7+ years).

list: Ultrasound if deep, or uncertain against a malformation or soft-tissue mass. MRI for complex facial or segmental lesions.
Abdominal ultrasound if there are 5 or more skin lesions.

head: Look-alike
Distinguishing clues
rows: Present at birth, flat, **grows with the child**, no rapid tumour growth
Fully formed at birth; different natural history
Later onset; often a pedunculated bleeding papule

management: Active observation with **photo documentation**. Reassure parents about involution.

management.h: Refer promptly (ideally by about 4 weeks of age if high risk)

list: Nasal tip, large facial, or **segmental** (PHACE risk with large facial segmental lesions)

Oral **propranolol** is first line for problematic IH. It is started and supervised by a specialist, with heart rate, BP and glucose monitoring. Feed regularly, and **hold doses if the baby is unwell or not feeding**.
Topical **timolol** for selected small, thin, superficial lesions (off-label; NICE ESUOM47).
Wound care, analgesia and antibiotics for ulceration; laser or surgery for selected residual changes.

red_flags: High-risk haemangioma sites (listed above): **do not wait to see if it goes away**.
Stridor or noisy breathing with a beard-area haemangioma: **urgent**.
pearls: The rapid growth window is early, so **late referral misses the easiest window for treatment**.
IP role: recognise high-risk sites, explain that beta-blockers are specialist-supervised, and support dressings for ulceration under the specialist plan.
BAD patient leaflet and the Birthmark Support Group are useful for families.
